newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Fischler criticises Germany on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Fischler criticises Germany on EMU.

text.p: European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler criticised Germany's stand on European monetary union in a newspaper interview published on Tuesday, saying Bonn ran the risk of becoming isolated from the rest of Europe.

Fischler, a former Austrian agriculture minister, told the Austrian daily Kurier that Bonn's hardline position on European economic and monetary union (EMU) and its adherence to a so-called stability pact may be counter-productive.
"I'm not sure whether a stability pact is likely to come to anything. That depends on the Germans," he told the Kurier.
"If they (the Germans) remain stubborn, that will be a problem," he said as Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Jacques Chirac met for a Franco-German summit in Nuremberg.

"Germany is gradually becoming isolated with its hardline position," he said, noting that the European Commission did not support automatic sanctions against countries breaching the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product by 1997.
EU ministers should decide every case on an individual basis, Fischler said.

France and Germany on Monday launched a joint initiative to reform the European Union, calling for closer cooperation on police, justice, foreign affairs and defence, and a shakeup of EU institutions.

But a Franco-German letter to fellow EU leaders ahead of Friday's summit in Dublin left key issues vague, and the two nations apparently failed to bridge differences on a "stability pact" to strengthen a future single European currency.

Germany has found itself at odds with France and other EU countries on the terms of the stability pact, intended to ensure countries entering the European economic and monetary union in 1999 keep budget spending under control.

Fischler, in Vienna on Monday for a conference on rural development, told reporters he was determined the next round of global negotiations on the liberalisation of agricultural products should not begin before 1999.

"We (European Union countries) are not strictly against liberalisation, but against uncontrolled liberalisation and in favour of multi-functional agriculture," he said on the first day of the World Trade Organisation summit in Singapore.
He said issues such as protection of the landscape and responsibility for bio-diversity needed to be addressed in conjunction with liberalisation.
